newsitem.title: USA: Sex probe of Army school grows with hotline calls.
newsitem.headline: Sex probe of Army school grows with hotline calls.

text.p: More than 100 reports of sexual harassment at the U.S. Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground are under investigation as a result of a hotline established in the midst of a growing scandal, a spokesman said Thursday.

Some 6,107 calls were received on the hotline as of Tuesday from throughout the Army and 849 cases were "deemed to warrant further investigation," of which 121 cases were from the proving ground, officials said.

The hotline was set up in November to receive reports of sexual harassment after three trainers at the Army's training facility at Aberdeen were charged in the rape and sexual harrassment scandal. The accusations were followed by charges at other bases and a promise by military top brass to end sexual harassment in the Army.

In one of the other cases, a court martial was scheduled at Fort Leonard Wood in Missouri on Thursday for Staff Sgt. Anthony Fore, charged with failing to obey a general regulation, indecent assault, maltreatment and assault and battery. Another staff sergeant at Fort Leonard Wood pleaded guilty in November to seven charges of misconduct.

Aberdeen base spokesman George Mercer said he could not confirm a New York Times report that more than 25 drill sergeants and other instructors were now under investigation at Aberdeen. The Times said more than 50 women had said they were raped, assaulted or harassed at the training school.

Mercer said 20 soldiers were implicated there, including three trainers arraigned last week, 15 suspended from their duties pending investigation and two fined in connection with the probe. The initial investigation at Aberdeen involved harassment reports from 17 women.
Of the 121 hotline reports being investigated at the proving ground, 34 related to the school and 87 related to other proving ground activities, Mercer said.

In a tour of the base by a Congressional delegation on Wednesday, Representative Stephen Buyer, an Indiana Republican, suggested the sexual harassment problem was related to inviduals who needed to be removed from the military.

"If you have an individual that would abuse their authority for their own sexual gratification, that needs to be rooted out of the military," said Buyer, who headed the delegation. But others in the delegation said the Army needed to make clear that sexual harassment was not to be tolerated.
Trial dates for the three accused soldiers at Aberdeen have been set for early next year.
